summary: Discusses flows and the attributes they can have, to provide a logical framework for adding new attributes to traffic flow measurement. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: Each data flow has traits, like a car's color or size. This sets up a tidy way to add new traits worth tracking.

questions: how to add new traffic flow attributes
how does an rtfm meter store distributions
subtitle: A proposed framework for adding performance-style attributes such as packet-size distributions and bit rates to RTFM traffic meters.

tldr.problem: RTFM meters count bytes and packets per flow, but network operators also want performance measures such as packet sizes, inter-arrival times and short-term rates.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC groups new attributes into trace, aggregate and group classes, stores multi-valued ones as distributions of counters set up through the PushPkt rule's mask and value fields, and proposes attribute numbers for them.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental proposal that leaves the basic RTFM meter unchanged and says a companion document would define the MIB structures.

today: RFC 2724 is an Experimental memo, not an Internet standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: RTFM Flows and Why Extend Them
sections.content:
The Real-Time Flow Measurement (RTFM) Working Group developed a system for measuring and reporting traffic flows. This memo extends the flow measurements defined in the architecture document (RFC 2722) with attributes meant for monitoring network performance, beyond simple volume counts. A companion document is to define MIB structures for them.

A flow is a set of packets between two endpoints, and is bi-directional: the meter watches two sub-flows, one each way. A flow is fully identified by its endpoint attribute values, it has a LastTime, and it has two packet counters and two byte counters, Forward and Backward. Existing counters are never reset, and the RFC calls these "old-style" attributes.

The RFC also notes that a flow can change as it crosses routers and switches, so the location of the meter matters when reading attributes.
sections.eli5: A meter watches conversations between two computers and counts what goes each way. This memo asks what else it could count.

sections.title: Three Classes of Attributes
sections.content:
New performance attributes such as throughput, packet loss, delays, jitter and congestion measures fall into three classes:

  • Trace: attributes of individual packets, for example last packet size or arrival time.
  • Aggregate: derived from the flow as a whole, for example mean rate, maximum packet size or a packet size distribution.
  • Group: depend on groups of packet values, for example inter-arrival times and short-term traffic rates.

Aggregate attributes are simple extensions of old-style ones: their values are never reset, and a meter reader collects them at intervals so an analysis application can compute differences. Group attributes include short-term bit rate, inter-arrival times (an indication of jitter), turn-around statistics for opposite-direction packets, and subflow analysis such as counting TCP and UDP streams between two hosts.

The meter only produces an extended attribute when the Rule table explicitly says so. Packet traces are a low priority because the RMON MIB already provides them.
sections.eli5: You can note facts about single cars, about the whole traffic jam, or about how cars space themselves out.

sections.title: Types and Distributions
sections.content:
Old-style aggregate attributes use three types: addresses as byte strings of 1 to 20 bytes, counters as 64-bit unsigned integers, and times as 32-bit unsigned integers. Some new attributes need many values, such as one inter-packet interval per packet. The RFC offers two ways to store them: a distribution, an array of bucket counters between a minimum and maximum, which is compact and fits the goal of data reduction inside the meter, or a sequence of single values, which keeps everything but does not.

A distribution is read by a meter reader as one structured object: the mask and value fields from the creating rule, plus the counters (buckets plus overflow). Each direction gets its own distribution, as with toOctets and fromOctets.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing down every car, you keep tally boxes such as small, medium and large, and add a mark to the right box.

sections.title: Specifying Distributions in Rule Sets
sections.content:
No new architecture is needed. A distribution attribute is added with a PushPkt or PushPkttoAct action, and the unused mask and value fields of that rule, each at least six bytes, carry the parameters. The proposed layout is:

  • Mask byte 1: Transform, 1 for linear or 2 for logarithmic. Byte 2: Scale Factor, a power of 10 multiplier. Bytes 3-4: Lower Limit, the highest value for the first bucket. Bytes 5-6: Upper Limit, the highest value for the last bucket.
  • Value byte 1: number of buckets, not counting the overflow bucket. Bytes 2 to 6: Parameter-1, -2 and -3, whose use depends on the attribute.

Experiments with NeTraMet used a rule for packet size with 60 buckets covering 1 to 1500 bytes in steps of 25, plus an overflow bucket, so 61 counters. Another used a logarithmic array of 60 counters for inter-arrival times from 1 ms to 1.8 s, and a third used 60 counters for bit rates from 1 kbps to 10 Mbps computed every 5 seconds.
sections.eli5: Two small notes on the rule say how many tally boxes to use, how wide each is, and what counts as too big.

sections.title: Proposed Attribute Numbers
sections.content:
Value 65 is suggested for a "Distributions" attribute with one bit per distribution-valued attribute, starting with attribute 66. Ten distribution attributes were numbered by RTFM Working Group consensus at the 1997 meeting in Munich: packet size, interarrival time, turnaround time, bit rate and PDU rate, each with a To and From form. Numbers 76 to 97 are left for other distributions.

The RFC suggests numbers 98 to 106 for the Integrated Services attributes (QoSService, QoSStyle, QoSRate, QoSSlackTerm and the token bucket and peak rate items), which came from work at CEFRIEL. NetFlowMet, a version of the meter, implemented MeterID (112), SourceASN (113), SourcePrefix (114), DestASN (115) and DestPrefix (116). A DSCodePoint attribute (118) holds the 6-bit DS Code Point, and only one such attribute exists because the field is a single field in the IP header.
sections.eli5: Each new thing to count gets a number, like a locker number, so meters and readers agree on which is which.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The attributes are properties of traffic flows and do not present security issues in themselves. The RFC warns that the collected flow data could be of considerable value, so suitable precautions should be taken to keep it safe.
sections.eli5: The counts are harmless, but a record of who talked to whom is valuable, so lock it up.

items.text: Derived from the whole flow, such as mean rate or packet size distribution.
